_metadata.scope: Ancestors of interpreted items: Liber 1 Prologus (5 partes), Liber 1 Distinctio 37, Liber 2 Distinctio 44, Liber 1, Liber 2, and the whole work. Libri 3-4 and all other divisions have no interpreted descendants and are omitted.

jdso8u-d1e71.summary: Part 1 of the Prologue: the necessity of supernaturally revealed doctrine. Its one question asks whether man in the present state needs a doctrine he cannot reach by natural light. Against philosophers who hold nature sufficient, Scotus argues that natural reason cannot know man's end distinctly, the means to it (which depend on God's contingent acceptance of merit), or what is proper to separate substances and to God as triune. He defines revelation as supernatural because its agent is not a natural mover of our intellect and stands in for a supernatural object. God is man's natural end, attainable only supernaturally, for which the intellect has a natural passive capacity.
claims: Supernaturally revealed doctrine is necessary for man in the present state.
Man cannot naturally know his end, the means to it, or the proper features of God and separate substances.
God is man's natural end, attainable only supernaturally.

jdso8u-d1e88.summary: Part 2 of the Prologue: the sufficiency of Scripture. Scotus defends the truth of the canon against those who reject all or part of it through ten rational motives of credibility (prophecy, concord of the writers, their veracity, the care of the receiving communities, reasonableness of content, the irrationality of rival errors, the Church's stability, miracles, outsiders' testimony, the constancy of sincere seekers), with sharply polemical treatment of other religions. He then argues that Scripture sufficiently contains what the wayfarer needs: man's particular end, the commandments as means, and their sufficiency, with further truths virtually contained in it and drawn out by interpreters.
claims: The truth of Scripture is supported by rational motives of credibility.
Scripture sufficiently contains the supernatural doctrine the wayfarer needs.
Necessary truths not explicit in Scripture are virtually contained in it.

jdso8u-d1e105.summary: Part 3 of the Prologue: the subject of theology. This summary rests on the one transcribed item, which covers all three questions of this part (the other two EDF items are deprecated placeholders). Scotus distinguishes theology in itself from theology in us and defines a first subject as what first and virtually contains all the truths of a science. The first subject of theology in itself is God as this essence (ut haec), not under a common concept, an attribute, or a relation such as restorer; neither Christ nor man is the first subject. For us, lacking evidence from the object, the first known subject is infinite being. He also argues that metaphysics concerns being as being, and that God's theology covers all knowables, while ours is limited to Scripture and what follows from it.
claims: The first subject of theology in itself is God as this essence.
Our theology's subject is the same essence, conceived by us at best as infinite being.
Neither Christ nor man is theology's first subject.
Our theology is limited to Scripture and what is derivable from it.
concepts: theology in itself and in us

jdso8u-d1e144.summary: Part 4 of the Prologue: whether theology is a science and whether it is subalternated. Measured against the four Aristotelian conditions of science, theology in itself meets all but discursive causation, while the blessed can have it with all four. Since evidence and certainty, not the necessity of the object, make cognition perfect, theological contingents seen in God are known more perfectly than acquired science, and theology is better called wisdom. Theology in itself is neither subalternated nor subalternating, and Scotus argues against the view that our theology is subalternated to the science of God and the blessed.
claims: Theology in itself is a science in all conditions but discursive causation, and better called wisdom.
Evidence and certainty, not necessity of object, constitute the perfection of cognition.
Theology is neither subalternated nor subalternating.

jdso8u-d1e162.summary: Part 5 of the Prologue: whether theology is practical. This summary rests on the one transcribed item, which covers both questions of this part (the other EDF item is a deprecated placeholder). Scotus defines praxis as primarily the will's elicited act, conformable to right reason, and holds that knowledge is practical by aptitudinal conformity and natural priority to right volition, grounded in its object rather than its end. All necessary theology in a created intellect is therefore practical, since its first subject contains the principles of right love, and love of the end is free and can be right or wrong. Theology of contingents is per se speculative but accidentally practical for creatures, and God's own theology is probably not practical, his will being its own rule.
claims: Praxis is primarily the elicited act of will.
Knowledge is practical from its object, not its end.
All necessary theology in a created intellect is practical.
God's own theology is probably not practical.

jdso8u-d1e1288.summary: Book I, distinction 37 (single question): whether God's omnipotence entails his immensity. Against the Aristotelian principle that an agent must be present to what it acts on, Scotus argues that this need comes from features of imperfect created agents. Omnipotence acts by will, which can will the distant as readily as the near, and at creation God's power did not presuppose his essential presence anywhere. So omnipotence does not entail immensity: God is everywhere, but this cannot be proved from his power to act everywhere.
claims: Omnipotence does not entail immensity.
Presence by power is prior to and independent of presence by essence.
The agent-patient contact principle holds only for natural agents.

jdso8u-d1e2347.summary: Book II, distinction 44 (single question, closing book II): whether the power of sinning is from God. Scotus distinguishes the power as a relation from its foundation. The relation to sin's deformity is nothing and is not from God; the relation to the underlying positive act is from God. The foundation is the free, defectible will, which causes rectitude effectively and sin defectively, and as a positive being it is from God. Anselm's claim that ability to sin is no part of freedom holds of freedom as a pure perfection; ability to sin follows from the limitation of created freedom.
claims: The power of sinning, as its positive foundation (the free will), is from God.
Sin's formal deformity is nothing and not from God.
Ability to sin follows from the limitation of created freedom, not from freedom as such.

jdso8u-d1e66.summary: The Prologue to the Ordinatio, a sustained account of what theology is. All five parts are covered (two are marked partial only because of deprecated, empty placeholder items in the EDF). Part 1 argues that supernatural revelation is necessary because natural reason cannot know man's end, the means to it, or God as he is in himself. Part 2 argues that Scripture is credible and sufficient for the wayfarer. Part 3 identifies theology's first subject as God as this essence (for us, conceived as infinite being), distinguishing theology in itself from theology in us. Part 4 holds that theology in itself is a science, better called wisdom, and is neither subalternated nor subalternating. Part 5 argues that theology is practical, since it directs the free love of God. Running through the Prologue are a critique of the philosophers' confidence in the sufficiency of nature, the distinction between theology in itself and in us, and the centrality of the will and of God's contingent willing.
claims: Revealed theology is necessary because natural reason cannot reach man's supernatural end or God as he is.
Scripture is credible and sufficient for the wayfarer.
Theology's first subject is God as this essence.
Theology in itself is a science, better called wisdom, and is not subalternated.
Theology is a practical science because it directs the will's love of God.
concepts: theology in itself and in us

jdso8u-d1e61.summary: Book I of the Ordinatio, which treats God, covered here only partially: this summary rests on the Prologue and distinction 37 alone, and the other 42 divisions of book I are not yet interpreted. The Prologue establishes what theology is: necessary because natural reason cannot reach man's supernatural end, contained in a credible and sufficient Scripture, having God as this essence as its subject, a science better called wisdom, and practical because it directs the free love of God. Distinction 37 argues that God's omnipotence does not entail his immensity, since an agent acting by will is not bound by the need for contact that limits natural agents. Together they show recurrent Scotist themes: the limits of natural reason, the primacy of the will and of God's free, contingent action, and resistance to deriving divine attributes from the pattern of natural causes.
claims: Revealed theology is necessary and practical, with God as this essence as its subject.
Omnipotence does not entail immensity, since God acts by will.

jdso8u-d1e1478.summary: Book II of the Ordinatio, which treats creation and creatures, covered here only by its final distinction 44; the other 25 divisions are not yet interpreted. That distinction asks whether the power of sinning is from God and answers that, as a positive foundation (the free, defectible created will), it is from God, while sin's formal deformity is nothing and not from God. The ability to sin is traced to the limitation of created freedom, not to freedom as a pure perfection, which shows Scotus's concern to keep God the source of all positive being in creatures without making him the author of sin.
claims: The power of sinning, as the free will, is from God; sin's deformity is not.
Ability to sin follows from the limitation of created freedom.

jdso8u.summary: John Duns Scotus, Ordinatio, a commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences in four books. This summary rests on a very small subset: the Prologue and distinction 37 of book I and distinction 44 of book II. Books III and IV and nearly all other distinctions are not yet interpreted, so it should not be read as a summary of the whole work. In the covered parts, the Prologue sets out Scotus's conception of theology (necessary beyond natural reason, grounded in Scripture, having God as this essence as its subject, and practical because it directs the will's love of God). I d.37 denies that omnipotence entails immensity. II d.44 locates the power to sin in the free, defectible created will, which as positive being is from God. Common threads are the limits of natural reason and the central role of will, divine and created.
claims: Theology is necessary beyond natural reason and is practical, ordered to the love of God.
God's power, exercised by will, does not entail his essential presence everywhere.
The created will's ability to sin follows from its limitation, while its positive being is from God.
